high-altitude-cruise — High altitude cruise

Above 10,000 ft the physiological environment becomes the limiting factor. Time of useful consciousness falls from around 20 minutes at 18,000 ft to well under a minute above 35,000 ft. Hypoxia is dangerous because its onset is comfortable: euphoria, poor judgement and slowed reaction arrive before any sense of breathlessness. The victim often feels fine. Know the aircraft's oxygen or pressurisation system and check it before departure rather than when needed. In a pressurisation failure, the sequence is oxygen mask on first, then an emergency descent, then communicate. Cruise altitude selection trades against wind. A higher level offers lower fuel flow and better true airspeed, but the jet stream can impose a headwind that outweighs both. The winds-aloft forecast decides which level is fastest.

density-altitude — Density altitude

Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for temperature, and it is what the aircraft actually feels. High elevation, high temperature and high humidity each reduce air density, and their effects combine. Consequences are simultaneous and all unfavourable: the engine produces less power, the propeller is less efficient, and the wing needs a higher true airspeed for the same lift. Takeoff roll lengthens, climb rate falls and the service ceiling drops. An airfield at 5,000 ft on a hot afternoon can behave like 8,000 ft or more. Performance charts assume a standard atmosphere, so the correction is not optional. Plan departures for early morning where possible, reduce weight rather than hope, and compute the actual takeoff distance for the actual conditions against the actual runway length.

engine-failure — Engine failure in flight

The order is fixed: fly the aircraft, pick a field, then troubleshoot. Pilots have flown serviceable aircraft into the ground while working a checklist. Establish best glide speed immediately and trim for it. Best glide is a specific number for the aircraft and weight, and both faster and slower reduce the distance available. Choose a landing site while altitude still offers a choice, favouring into-wind, long, smooth and unobstructed over merely close. Commit early; changing target late costs more than the imperfection of the first choice. Then run the restart flow: fuel selector to a tank with fuel, mixture rich, carburettor heat on, ignition on both, boost pump as fitted. Declare an emergency. Squawk 7700. Secure fuel and ignition before touch down, keep the shoulder harness tight, and fly the aircraft all the way into the crash.

emergency-descent — Emergency descent

An emergency descent is warranted by pressurisation failure, an uncontrolled fire, or any condition where remaining at altitude is more dangerous than descending rapidly. With a pressurisation failure the order is oxygen first. Consciousness is the prerequisite for everything else, and time of useful consciousness at high altitude is measured in seconds. Then descend at the maximum rate the airframe allows: power to idle, speed brakes as fitted, and a bank to increase the rate while keeping the speed within limits. In turbulence or with suspected structural damage, use a lower speed -- a rapid descent that overstresses the airframe has solved nothing. Level off at a safe altitude. 10,000 ft is standard where terrain allows, and the minimum safe altitude for the sector where it does not. Declare the emergency and squawk 7700.
